extracted.intended_audience: trademark practitioners, IP judges, patent/trademark office examiners, and IP litigators (Korea; comparative reference to US/EU/Japan)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/practical criteria and guidelines for evaluating distinctiveness, functionality, likelihood of confusion, unfair competition, and registrability of three-dimensional trademarks (product shapes and packaging), with Korean Supreme Court precedent and KIPO functionality guidelines and comparative notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Trademark Act Article 6(1)(iii) (indication of product shape)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indication of shape of a product or its packaging, regulated by Trademark Act Article 6(1)(iii), is applicable where the outer appearance, shape (including patterns), and size directly indicate the general form of the designated product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For three-dimensional trademarks this applies if the outer appearance of the product or its packaging expresses the general form of the product. Even partial changes or additional decorations do not confer distinctiveness if they merely contribute to product functions or aesthetic sensibility and fail to go beyond a scope that can be adopted generally in trade. (Examples: cylinder glue-stick container; building-block shapes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquired distinctiveness under Trademark Act Article 6(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark that would otherwise fall under Article 6(1)(iii) (or 6(1)(v)/(vi)) can be registered if consumers prominently/clearly recognize it as indicating the product of a specific business owner due to use prior to the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Article 6(2) grants an exclusive right for marks originally lacking intrinsic distinctiveness, its criteria must be stringently interpreted and applied: clear evidence is required that the trademark itself is clearly recognized by consumers. Consideration should be comprehensive and strict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for assessing acquired distinctiveness of three-dimensional shapes
rubrics_metrics.description: To evaluate whether a three-dimensional shape has obtained acquired distinctiveness, consider characteristics of the shape, period and duration of use, sales quantity and market share, duration and size of advertisements and promotions, magnitude of competitive use with other similar-formed products, and the reputation and credit of the trademark user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess these factors in a comprehensive manner and apply stringent interpretation. If the shape is accompanied by attached marks (symbols/characters), consider outer appearance, size, location of attachment, and level of recognition of the attached mark to determine whether the shape itself independently indicates source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionality prohibition under Trademark Act Article 7(1)(xiii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 7(1)(xiii) prohibits registration of a trademark that consists only of a three-dimensional shape that is indispensable for acquiring the technical functions of the product (i.e., functional shapes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule prevents trademarks from granting permanent exclusive rights over technical functions that should be protected (if at all) by patent/utility model or design rights. In determining functionality, consider whether there are alternative shapes usable or on the market, whether production cost is equivalent or lower with an alternative shape, and whether the shape exerts technical superiority beyond the product's intrinsic function. Evaluate comprehensively to avoid impeding competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfair competition protection for product shapes (secondary meaning / prominence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even absent IP rights, a product shape may be protected under the Unfair Competition Protection Act if it acquires a secondary function of indicating source and attains prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For protection, the shape must have unique design characteristics that strongly appeal to consumers' senses compared with similar products; possess a certain level of distinctiveness so general consumers can recognize the specific business owner at a glance; and be used continuously, monopolistically, and exclusively for a long time, or be subject to strong promotions/advertisements (even over a short period) that explicitly individualize its discriminative characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity evaluation of trademarks (three aspects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity ought to be evaluated objectively, comprehensively, and detachedly by observing trademarks in three aspects: outer appearance, name, and concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assess similarity by mere juxtaposition. Consider different times and places to determine how consumers encountering the marks might form impressions, memories, and associations. If the aggregated impressions (appearance, name, concept) can cause mistaken recognition or confusion as to the product source, they are similar. Pay special attention to dominant impressions of three-dimensional trademarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of text marks, packaging text, and trade channels on similarity/confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of names, text marks, company names on packaging and the product, and the distribution channel (e.g., prescription-only products provided by pharmacists) affect the likelihood of confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in packaging text or prominent text marks can reduce similarity/confusion. In professional channels (doctors/pharmacists), consumers are less likely to be confused by product shape alone; prescription contexts reduce the likelihood of confusion even when shapes/colors are similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: KIPO functionality guideline: Substitutability
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether there are other shapes that can substitute the three-dimensional shape. A trademark lacks functionality if multiple other shapes can be used as substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: if the shape is intrinsic to the purpose and usage of the product, it may be evaluated as having functionality even if multiple shapes exist. Consider market-available alternatives in the specific product market.

rubrics_metrics.name: KIPO functionality guideline: Inexpensiveness of production cost
rubrics_metrics.description: If the production cost for the registered shape is lower than alternatives, or the production process is so simple that free competition using other substitutable shapes is limited, the three-dimensional shape is viewed to have functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functionality is supported if there are advertisements/promotions emphasizing reduced production cost or simplified production process. Assess whether cost/production considerations would create a competitive advantage amounting to utilitarian functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: KIPO functionality guideline: Existence of patents or utility models
rubrics_metrics.description: If there were or are patents or utility models about the three-dimensional shape, the shape can be viewed to have functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of patent/utility-model protection for the shape is strong indicia of utilitarian function; consult patent/utility model registers and assess technical disclosure overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: KIPO functionality guideline: Advertisements/promotions about distribution convenience and efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Functionality is acknowledged if significant convenience in preservation, transport, handling (distribution) derives from the product or its packaging, or if advertisements promote significant efficiency of use due to its shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider marketing materials and promotional claims that tout distribution or usage efficiencies; such evidence supports a finding of functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: KIPO functionality guideline: evaluation focus and comprehensive test
rubrics_metrics.description: Functionality evaluation should be based on whether the three-dimensional shape of the product or packaging is functional, not on whether the product itself is functional. The test is a comprehensive evaluation of whether the utilitarian advantage of the shape provides vast superiority in competition and whether monopoly of such shapes would unfairly disturb competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a registered trademark is considered to have functionality in general, it is evaluated as having functionality even if it includes some non-functional factors. The assessment requires weighing competitive effects and potential monopolization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stringent standard for proving acquired distinctiveness (case law guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 6(2) relief (acquired distinctiveness) is to be strictly applied: even substantial sales/market share does not alone prove that the shape has been used consistently as the trademark or that consumers recognize the shape as the source indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require evidence that the particular shape has been used as the trademark (i.e., consistent use of the exact shape), not merely that products were sold by the plaintiff in the market. High market share, advertising, and use of word marks do not substitute for evidence of consumer recognition of the shape itself (examples: glue-stick and building-block precedents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent indicators for denying distinctiveness in three-dimensional marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Marks that express the quality, utility, use, or shape of the designated product in a generally used method are descriptive and typically rejected (Article 6(1)(iii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the shape is a general/form commonly used for that product class (e.g., typical pill shapes, common vacuum cleaner forms), courts have denied distinctiveness. Consider whether the shape is indispensable or generally used in the trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative foreign principles on functionality (US/EU/Japan)
rubrics_metrics.description: US PTO and case law consider presence of patents, advertisements promoting utilitarian advantages, whether registration would disturb competition, and presence of substitutable shapes. EC rules prohibit shapes deriving from the intrinsic property of the product, shapes required to obtain a technical result, or shapes that provide practical value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Korean evaluations reflect similar concerns and look to foreign precedents (US/EU/Japan) as comparative guidance. Use foreign principles when analyzing functionality, but apply Korean statutory text and KIPO guidelines for domestic cases.
